title: Open Knowledge Austria is back
content:
AI is making data more valuable than ever. Yet AI crawlers are threatening the open data commons built over decades.

This pressure is already visible. Wikimedia reported in April 2025 that multimedia download bandwidth had grown by 50% since January 2024, largely because of automated scraping. Read the Docs reported in July 2024 that a single crawler downloaded 73 TB in May, generating more than $5,000 in bandwidth charges and prompting it to block that crawler.

Open Knowledge Austria is back, with a new focus: open knowledge in the age of AI. We're relaunching Austria's chapter in the Open Knowledge Foundation network to help meet this challenge together.

Working with open data? Bring your project, questions or expertise. Civil society, researchers, developers, public institutions, industry and anyone curious about open knowledge are welcome.

  • Make open data visible, discoverable and integrated. Help people find datasets, connect them and put them to work.

    • Make open data visible, discoverable and integrated. Help people find datasets, connect them and put them to work.

  • Contribute to a sustainable open data-AI ecosystem. Support fair access for users as well as agents.

title: Open Knowledge Austria at the OKFN Network
content:
What can the Austrian chapter contribute to the Open Knowledge Network, and how can other chapters work with us? Our presentation for the network meeting on 3 November 2026 brings together the people, projects and priorities behind our new beginning.

The nine-slide presentation is available in English, directly on our website. It introduces our team, our signed MoU with the Open Knowledge Foundation, and our work on open data and AI.

Open the presentation

Share the slides: okat.at/slides/okat-network-2026/

The presentation introduces Daniel Dobriy, Shahrom Sohi and Alina Halaburda alongside Kremena Irinkova, our Network Manager for industry and research collaborations, and Bernhard Krabina, focusing on public organisations and MediaWiki. Together, we want to connect civil society, research and public institutions around practical uses of open knowledge.

  • Open Data Inside: a shared badge, ambassador directory and place to make projects using open data visible. Explore opendatainside.org/en.

title: Open Data Inside is back. Show what you build.
content:
A useful map. A public-interest investigation. A tool that turns a complicated dataset into something anyone can understand. Open data is often doing important work behind the scenes. Open Data Inside puts it on the label.

We are relaunching Open Data Inside to make that work easier to discover—and easier to join. The idea is simple: when open data helps make something possible, let people see it.

The project’s original badge launched in January 2015. Its purpose remains clear: give people and organisations using open data a recognisable way to show it. The renewed platform brings that idea together with a public ambassador directory and a route for submitting your own project.

Think about the distance between publishing a dataset and someone benefiting from it. Along the way are people cleaning it, explaining it, building applications, finding patterns, and asking better questions. Their work deserves to be visible. When reuse is visible, it becomes easier to explain why maintaining open data is worth the effort.

Open data has a story after the download. Let’s make that story visible.

title: Open Knowledge Austria starts anew
content:
Knowledge becomes useful when someone can question it, connect it to something else, and put it to work. That conviction brings us here: Open Knowledge Austria is starting anew.

We are building a new Austrian organisation for open data, shared knowledge, and technology that serves the public good. Our starting point is Vienna. Our invitation reaches anyone who wants to make information more accessible, understandable, and useful.

There is a history behind this beginning—and a changed world ahead of it.

The Austrian open knowledge community helped turn an ambitious idea into practical work. In a 2012 account for the Open Knowledge Foundation, Martin Kaltenböck traced the Open Knowledge Forum Austria’s beginnings to Vienna in early 2011. Its work included support for municipal open data portals, events, and cooperation across public administration, research, business, and civil society.

By the community’s 2016 update, that work encompassed open science, data literacy, Vienna Open Data Meetups, and the OpenDataPortal collaboration with Wikimedia Austria. These were people making openness useful in everyday practice.

Open Knowledge Forum Austria begins in Vienna.
